judge_assessment.explanation: The mathematics is exact and I recomputed all twelve checks: 7x²+3x−5x²+8x−2 = 2x²+11x−2; (5x²−3x+4)−(2x²+7x−6) = 3x²−10x+10; −3x(2x²−4x+5) = −6x³+12x²−15x; (4x²−6x+1)−(x²−2x−5) = 3x²−4x+6 with value 10 at x = 2; −2x(3x−7)+5(x−4) = −6x²+19x−20 with value −7 at x = 1; x²−5x−24 = (x−8)(x+3) with value −28 at x = 1; and (2x−3)² = 4x²−12x+9 with value 1 at x = 1. Each planted wrong line is reachable by the stated wrong method and lands on a different number (−8, −35, −18, 13), so the judge's 'planted wrong results are genuinely distinguishable' is correct and machine-proved. Problem 8 is correctly manual with a strong desc. Where I go beyond the verdict: the find-and-fix items are only half recorded. Problem 4 says 'Name the step that goes wrong', problem 5 says 'Exactly one term is mis-signed. Name it', and problem 7 says 'Decide whether they are' — three required responses that are a diagnosis in words, and verify.json ids 4, 5 and 7 carry only expand and eval entries with no manual flag. That is the canonical flag-open-response-as-manual shape: 'an item requiring an explanation, diagnosis, named error … recorded as machine-verified rather than manual'. The key does name each error in its solution, so the content is there; what is missing is the declaration that a human has to read those words, and final_response.md's 'Every algebraic answer was recomputed … Problem 8 is an open written response' understates the hand-grading this sheet needs by three items.

strengths_to_preserve: The three named misconceptions in the header — the stranded minus, the false like term, the missing middle term — are each instantiated twice: once as clean mechanics (problems 2, 1, 6) and once as a planted error to repair (4, 8, 7). The sheet teaches the rule and then makes the student prosecute it.

Every find-and-fix item ends in a substitution check at a NAMED value, and the values are chosen to separate the two expressions (x = 2 gives 10 against −8; x = 1 gives 1 against 13). The key even warns that x = 1 does NOT separate 3x²+5x from 8x², which is the subtlety that makes substitution checking a real technique rather than a ritual.

The 'common wrong answers' block prints a line for every planted mistake with the diagnosis attached ('If they got −8: distributed the subtraction sign to the first term only'), so a wrong answer tells the grader which rule failed.
Three pages for eight problems with the answer key at three pages: this is the most economical layout in the batch and the only one the judge did not mark down on print quality.

root_causes.description: A find-and-fix item has two answers — the corrected algebra and the NAME of the failing step — and only the first is representable in the verification record today. Because the corrected expression is checked, the id counts as covered and the diagnosis leaves no trace, even though it is the part the misconception-analysis format exists to elicit.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 4: 'Name the step that goes wrong, write the correct simplification, then evaluate …'; verify.json id 4 = one expand + one eval, no manual entry.
problem 5: 'Exactly one term is mis-signed. Name it, expand the left side correctly, then evaluate …'; id 5 = one expand + one eval.
problem 7: 'Decide whether they are, expand (2x−3)² correctly, and support your decision …'; id 7 = one equiv + one eval.

verify.json contains exactly one manual entry, on id 8, and gate_log records the build as green with manual flags present — so the chain cannot tell the difference between 'no open responses' and 'three undeclared ones'.

improvements.title: Require a manual entry for the diagnosis half of every find-and-fix item
improvements.proposed_change: Make the misconception-analysis pattern in references/problem-library.md specify TWO entries per find-and-fix item: the machine check on the corrected result, and a manual entry whose desc states what naming the error must contain (for problem 5: 'the +14x term — −2x times −7 is positive'). Add the gate that fails when a stem contains an imperative to name, identify, decide or explain and the id carries no manual entry. The answer key template should then print a 'Manual review:' acceptance line under those solutions, as it already does for problem 8.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture worksheet whose problem stem reads 'Exactly one term is mis-signed. Name it, expand the left side correctly, then evaluate your corrected answer at x = 1' with a verify.json id holding only expand and eval entries. The gate must exit non-zero naming the diagnosis; adding a manual entry must make it pass. Today this exact shape builds green — curr-254's gate_log.txt is the evidence.
improvements.expected_impact: The manual count on misconception sheets becomes truthful (4 items here rather than 1), and each named-error response reaches the grader with criteria instead of relying on the reader to infer them from the worked solution.
improvements.risk: Every misconception-analysis sheet gains manual entries, which lowers the machine-verified fraction these runs report. That is a reporting cosmetic, not a regression, but the summary line should distinguish 'verified answer, hand-read diagnosis' from 'unverified'.

case_summary: A focused, economical misconception packet with exact algebra: eight problems, twelve machine checks all recomputing correctly, four planted errors proved distinguishable from their corrections, and a key that names the specific rule each error breaks. The study guide's three sections map one-to-one onto the three errors the header declares. The gap is declarative rather than mathematical: problems 4, 5 and 7 each require the student to NAME the failing step or decide a claim, and those responses are recorded as fully machine-verified because the accompanying algebra is checked. Only problem 8 is flagged manual. final_response.md names all three PDFs, the bank prints a real value on every non-manual row, and the 32/32 verdict is defensible on the mathematics — the defect is that the verification record understates what a human must read.
